activities.anchor: architecture forced to say what it means
activities.caption: pair each consequence with what it buys
activities.name: cpConsequenceMatch

config.prompt: Four practical consequences of recording logic instead of results:

pairs.right: the BIM model is a parametric database — change the atrium, every section updates
a 12,000-panel facade gets its fabrication data automatically
the moments the model misbehaves are where your understanding was vague

config.why: Parametric modelling is architecture forced to say what it means — the quiet pedagogical power.

activities.caption: bet first — parametric without a single curve
activities.name: cpStraightPredict

config.q: Which of these is a genuine parametric-model task, with no curvy building in sight?
choices: Spacing a hospital's handrail brackets to code, every bay identical
Designing the Sagrada Família's hanging-chain vaults by hand
config.why: The tools are logic: optimising a repeated balcony section or testing a hundred rectangular school plans is the same method — the curvy style is separable, and confusing them costs the method its credibility.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the form-finding lineage
activities.name: cpLineageCloze

config.text: Gaudí's %%0%% models inverted gravity to find the pure compression shape; Frei Otto's %%1%% films computed minimal surfaces; and Gehry adopted %%2%% — an aerospace tool — to document Bilbao's titanium panels.
config.hint: Chains, films, and an aviation package — the constant is form found by simulating forces.

activities.anchor: never what the model cannot represent
activities.caption: rebuild the optimiser's honest sequence
activities.name: cpOptimiserOrder

config.prompt: From parametric model to chosen design — put the sequence in order:
items: Define constraints (site, code, budget) and objectives (daylight, area, carbon, cost)
The algorithm generates and scores thousands of candidates
It returns a Pareto front — no objective improves without another degrading
The human chooses among defensible designs
That choice of objectives IS the design ethics
config.why: Gradient methods need smooth objectives; architecture's problems are discrete and multi-objective — which is why evolutionary and genetic algorithms dominate.

activities.anchor: Optimisation relocates the judgement; it does not remove it
activities.caption: file the outputs — which optimum produced each?
activities.name: cpObjectiveBuckets

config.prompt: Two offices optimise the same site. File each outcome:

items.label: walls removed to let light reach every desk
the atrium shrunk for more lettable floor area
floor plate pushed shallow and wide
the plan stacked deep around a single core

config.why: Both 'optimal', both correct — the choice of objective function is a values decision made by a person.

activities.caption: true or false — the field's honest limits
activities.name: cpLimitsJudge

statements.s: The Pareto front is the set of designs where no objective improves without another degrading.
statements.why: Choosing a point on it remains irreducibly the designer's judgement.

statements.s: An algorithm told to maximise daylight will happily remove every wall.
statements.why: Objectives are proxies — the specification problem, architectural edition.

statements.s: Evolutionary algorithms dominate because design problems are discrete, multi-objective and non-differentiable.
statements.why: They mutate parameter sets, keep the fittest, and never need a gradient.

statements.s: The computer's optimum removes the designer's values decision.
statements.why: It relocates the judgement into the objective function — which is still a person's choice.
